title: Balancing Chemical Equations
seo_title: Balancing Equations Worksheets: Coefficients and Conservation of Mass (High School Chemistry)
standard_text: Use mathematical representations to support the claim that atoms, and therefore mass, are conserved during a chemical reaction.
meta_desc: Free high school chemistry worksheets on balancing chemical equations (NGSS HS-PS1-7): counting atoms, coefficients and subscripts, checking and balancing equations, and conservation of mass. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Balance with coefficients so each element has the same count on both sides.
body_html:
How to think about it

Atoms are rearranged, never created or destroyed.

  • Count every element on both sides. A coefficient multiplies every atom in its formula; a subscript outside parentheses multiplies everything inside.
  • Balance by changing only coefficients, never subscripts.
  • Total mass of reactants = total mass of products (in a closed system).
Example

Atoms of O in 3Ca(OH)2?

Each formula has 2 O

3 × 2

Answer: 6

Example

Balance ? H2 + O2 → 2H2O

4 H on the right

Answer: 2

Common mistakes

  • Changing subscripts to balance (H2O → H2O2).
  • Multiplying only the first atom by the coefficient.
  • Thinking mass is lost when a gas forms.

faq.q: How do you balance a chemical equation?
faq.a: Count the atoms of each element on both sides, then change coefficients (never subscripts) until every element matches.

faq.q: What is the difference between a coefficient and a subscript?
faq.a: A coefficient tells how many molecules or formula units. A subscript tells how many atoms are in one formula.
The same atoms are only rearranged into new substances, so the total mass stays the same in a closed system.
